questions.stem: William James described consciousness as a 'stream' because:
options: it stays at one fixed level of awareness throughout the day
it can only be experienced while a person is fully asleep
it is made of separate states that never connect together
thoughts and sensations flow continuously and keep changing
questions.explanation: James argued that conscious experience is continuous and ever-changing, like a stream, rather than a series of separate pieces.

questions.stem: The continuum of consciousness ranges from:
options: controlled processes to divided attention only
REM sleep at one end to light NREM sleep at the other
total awareness to a complete lack of awareness
normal waking consciousness to daydreaming only
questions.explanation: Consciousness is described as a continuum from total awareness (focused attention) through normal waking consciousness and altered states to a complete lack of awareness, such as unconsciousness or coma.

questions.stem: Compared with normal waking consciousness, an altered state of consciousness (ASC) is best described as:
options: a state in which a person has no awareness at all of anything
a state differing markedly in awareness, perception or thinking
a state in which awareness is always much higher than normal
a state that can only be reached through drugs or alcohol
questions.explanation: An ASC is any state that differs distinctly from normal waking consciousness in awareness, perception, thought, emotion or self-control. ASCs can be natural (sleep, daydreaming) or induced (alcohol).

questions.stem: A student in class drifts into thinking about her weekend and does not hear the teacher's question. In this daydream, her:
options: self-control is completely lost
perception is severely distorted
content is limited to the lesson
awareness of external events is reduced
questions.explanation: In daydreaming, attention shifts from external stimuli to internal thoughts, so awareness of surroundings decreases. Self-control is only mildly reduced and perception is not markedly distorted.

questions.stem: Which change is typical of alcohol-induced alteration of consciousness?
options: stronger memory for events that occur while drinking
reduced self-control and slowed reaction times
sharper perception and faster decision-making
increased ability to divide attention between tasks
questions.explanation: Alcohol depresses the central nervous system, reducing self-control and inhibition, slowing reactions and impairing perception, coordination, memory and judgement.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an automatic process?
options: a learner driver merging onto a freeway for the first time
a student solving an unfamiliar algebra problem
a person following new directions to a strange address
an experienced typist typing a familiar sentence
questions.explanation: Automatic processes require little attention, can be done alongside other tasks and are usually highly practised. The other tasks are new or complex, so they need controlled processing.

questions.stem: Which comparison of controlled and automatic processes is correct?
options: Controlled processes need little attention and are easy to combine with others
Automatic processes need focused attention and are slow and effortful to do
Automatic processes cannot ever develop from controlled processes with practice
Controlled processes need focused attention and are hard to combine with others
questions.explanation: Controlled processes require conscious, focused attention, are slower and interfere with other tasks. With practice, many controlled processes become automatic.

questions.stem: During an altered state, a person loses track of how much time has passed. Which characteristic of consciousness has changed?
options: time orientation
content limitation
emotional awareness
selective attention
questions.explanation: Time orientation is a person's awareness of the passage of time. In many ASCs, such as daydreaming or alcohol intoxication, time may seem to pass faster or slower than it really does.

questions.stem: At a noisy party, a person can follow one conversation while ignoring others, but notices when someone across the room says her name. This shows:
options: automatic processing
time orientation
selective attention
divided attention
questions.explanation: Selective attention focuses on one stimulus while filtering out others; this example is known as the cocktail party effect. Hearing her name shows unattended information is still monitored to some extent.

questions.stem: Why do drivers using a phone, even hands-free, make more errors than drivers who are not?
options: Selective attention allows drivers to focus fully on both the road and the call
Automatic processes cannot be used while a person is driving a car on the road
Hands-free phones increase drivers' awareness of the passage of time
Dividing attention between two tasks that need controlled processing hurts performance
questions.explanation: Attention is limited, so when two tasks both require controlled processing, dividing attention between them reduces performance on at least one. Highly practised automatic tasks are easier to combine.

questions.stem: In a sleep laboratory, electrodes on the scalp are connected to an electroencephalograph (EEG). This device detects:
options: the electrical activity of the brain
the electrical activity of the muscles
the movement of the eyes during sleep
the electrical conductivity of the skin
questions.explanation: An EEG detects and records brainwaves through electrodes on the scalp. Muscle activity is measured by an EMG, eye movements by an EOG and skin conductivity by GSR.

questions.stem: An electro-oculargraph (EOG) is used in sleep research to detect:
options: heart rate changes
eye movements
muscle tension
brainwave patterns
questions.explanation: An EOG records the electrical activity of the muscles that move the eyes. It is important for identifying REM sleep, which is defined by rapid eye movements.

questions.stem: Galvanic skin response (GSR) measures changes in the electrical conductivity of the skin. What does a higher GSR reading indicate?
options: deep relaxation and decreased alertness
rapid eye movements during dreaming
lower body temperature during deep sleep
increased sweating, a sign of higher arousal
questions.explanation: When arousal increases, sweat glands become more active, and moist skin conducts electricity better. GSR is therefore used as a measure of physiological arousal.

questions.stem: In a sleep laboratory, an EMG recording shows almost no muscle activity while an EOG shows bursts of rapid eye movement. The sleeper is most likely in:
options: REM sleep
light NREM sleep
deep NREM sleep
a relaxed waking state
questions.explanation: REM sleep combines rapid eye movements with near loss of tone in the major skeletal muscles, sometimes called sleep paralysis. NREM sleep has some muscle tone and few eye movements.

questions.stem: Why might a sleep researcher ask participants to keep a sleep diary as well as recording EEG data?
options: Self-reports capture experiences, such as dreams, that EEG cannot
Self-reports are more objective than physiological measures such as EEG
Self-reports can record brainwave activity while the person is asleep
Self-reports remove the need for any informed consent from participants
questions.explanation: Self-reports such as diaries capture subjective experiences, habits and dream content that physiological measures cannot. They are open to memory errors and bias, so they are combined with objective measures.

questions.stem: Which brainwave pattern is typical of a person who is awake, relaxed and has their eyes closed?
options: alpha waves
beta waves
delta waves
sleep spindles
questions.explanation: Alpha waves (regular, medium frequency) occur in relaxed wakefulness, especially with the eyes closed. Beta waves occur in alert, active thinking, and delta waves in deep NREM sleep.

questions.stem: Which feature is most characteristic of deep NREM sleep?
options: low-amplitude, irregular beta-like waves and rapid eye movements
alpha waves and frequent awareness of the surrounding room
sleep spindles and K-complexes only, with no delta waves
high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves and difficulty waking
questions.explanation: Deep NREM (slow-wave) sleep is dominated by delta waves, which are large and slow, and the sleeper is very hard to wake. Rapid eye movements and beta-like waves are features of REM sleep.

questions.stem: Sleep spindles and K-complexes appear on an EEG during:
options: REM sleep
relaxed wakefulness
alert wakefulness
NREM stage 2
questions.explanation: Sleep spindles (brief bursts of high-frequency waves) and K-complexes (single large waves) are the markers of stage 2 NREM sleep.

questions.stem: A student reads that REM sleep is a 'paradox'. Which feature of REM sleep does this label refer to?
options: Heart rate falls steadily, yet the sleeper's muscles are tense
Brain activity resembles waking, yet the body is nearly paralysed
Brain activity stops completely, yet the eyes move rapidly
The sleeper is easy to wake, yet brainwaves are very slow
questions.explanation: During REM sleep, EEG activity is fast and irregular like waking, and heart rate and breathing become irregular, yet the major skeletal muscles are almost completely relaxed.

questions.stem: Over a typical night of sleep, how do the stages change?
options: Deep NREM sleep mostly occurs early; REM periods get longer towards morning
REM sleep mostly occurs early; deep NREM periods get longer towards morning
Each cycle is identical, with the same amount of every stage across the night
Sleep goes through the stages only once, from light NREM to REM at dawn
questions.explanation: Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes. Deep NREM sleep dominates the first cycles, while later cycles contain little deep sleep and longer REM periods.

questions.stem: How does the proportion of REM sleep change across the lifespan?
options: It is highest in newborns and decreases into adulthood
It is lowest in newborns and increases into old age
It stays the same from infancy to old age in everyone
It is highest in adolescence and lowest in infancy
questions.explanation: Newborns spend about half their sleep in REM, compared with about 20 to 25 per cent in adults. The high proportion in infancy may support brain development.

questions.stem: A student sleeps only four hours a night for a week. This is:
options: total sleep deprivation
REM rebound
a microsleep
partial sleep deprivation
questions.explanation: Partial sleep deprivation is getting less sleep than normally needed. Total sleep deprivation is going without any sleep at all for a period.

questions.stem: A microsleep is:
options: a period of REM sleep that occurs early in the night
the short delay between lying down and falling asleep
a brief, involuntary sleep lasting a few seconds
a short nap taken deliberately in the early afternoon
questions.explanation: Microsleeps are brief, involuntary episodes of sleep, lasting from a fraction of a second to several seconds, that occur in sleep-deprived people. They are dangerous when driving.

questions.stem: Participants are woken each time they enter REM sleep for several nights. When finally allowed to sleep normally, they spend more time than usual in REM. This is:
options: REM rebound
a microsleep
sleep debt repayment in NREM
a delayed sleep phase
questions.explanation: REM rebound is the increase in REM sleep after a period of REM deprivation. It suggests REM sleep serves a function the body tries to make up.

questions.stem: After a period of total sleep deprivation, which recovery pattern is typical?
options: People recover only by sleeping longer in light stage 1 sleep each night
People cannot recover at all, and permanent cognitive damage always occurs
People do not recover all lost hours; extra deep NREM and REM sleep occurs
People must sleep for exactly as many hours as they lost before they recover
questions.explanation: Recovery sleep is usually only somewhat longer than normal. The lost time is not fully made up; instead the proportion of deep NREM and REM sleep increases, and most effects disappear after one or two nights.

questions.stem: Which effect is typical of sleep deprivation?
options: irritability, poor concentration and slower reactions
better mood, sharper attention and faster reaction times
improved memory and more creative problem-solving ability
no noticeable effect until after two weeks without sleep
questions.explanation: Even one night of lost sleep impairs mood, attention, concentration and reaction time. Longer deprivation adds microsleeps, memory problems and sometimes perceptual distortions.

questions.stem: Why do many adolescents find it hard to fall asleep before about 11 pm?
options: Melatonin is released later in the evening than in children
Melatonin is released earlier in the evening than in adults
Adolescents need much less sleep than children or adults
Adolescents have no circadian rhythm until they turn 18
questions.explanation: During adolescence the sleep-wake cycle shifts later (a delayed sleep phase), partly because melatonin is released later at night. Adolescents still need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

questions.stem: A Year 12 student must wake at 6.30 am for school but cannot fall asleep before 11.30 pm. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Total sleep deprivation, because she gets no sleep on school nights
Increased REM sleep, because adolescents need less deep NREM sleep
Better concentration, because adolescents need only about 6 hours
Chronic partial sleep deprivation, as she gets less sleep than needed
questions.explanation: She gets about 7 hours, less than the 8 to 10 hours adolescents need, so over weeks she builds up partial sleep deprivation. This can affect mood, attention and learning.

questions.stem: Which statement summarises the restoration theory of why we sleep?
options: Sleep lets the brain fulfil its unconscious wishes
Sleep lets the brain forget unwanted connections
Sleep lets the body and brain repair and recover
Sleep keeps animals hidden and safe during the night
questions.explanation: Restoration theory proposes that sleep allows the body to repair tissue, release growth hormone and replenish resources used while awake. Keeping animals safe is the survival theory.

questions.stem: Which observation is most difficult for the restoration theory of sleep to explain?
options: Deep NREM sleep increases after a period of sleep deprivation
Wounds and tissues heal faster when people get enough sleep
People need little extra sleep after a day of hard physical work
Growth hormone is mainly released during deep NREM sleep
questions.explanation: If sleep mainly repairs the body, very active days should greatly increase sleep need, but they increase it only slightly. The other observations support restoration theory.

questions.stem: The survival (evolutionary) theory proposes that sleep evolved to:
options: allow the mind to work through problems from waking life
remove unwanted memories that build up during the day
keep animals inactive and safe when activity is risky
allow the brain to repair cells damaged during the day
questions.explanation: Survival theory proposes that sleeping when activity is dangerous or unproductive, such as at night for humans, protected animals and conserved energy.

questions.stem: According to Freud, the hidden meaning of a dream, as opposed to the storyline remembered on waking, is its:
options: manifest content
activation
synthesis
latent content
questions.explanation: Freud distinguished the manifest content (the remembered storyline) from the latent content (the hidden, unconscious wishes it disguises). He saw dreams as wish fulfilment.

questions.stem: Hobson and McCarley's (1977) activation-synthesis theory proposes that dreams result from:
options: continued work on problems and concerns from waking life
the removal of unwanted connections in the cortex
the cortex making sense of random brainstem signals
unconscious wishes disguised as symbols to protect sleep
questions.explanation: In activation-synthesis theory, the pons fires random signals during REM sleep (activation) and the cortex combines them into a story (synthesis). It is a biological view.

questions.stem: Cartwright found that people going through a divorce often dreamed about their relationship and coping. Which theory of dreaming does this support?
options: activation-synthesis theory
reverse learning theory
restoration theory
problem-solving theory
questions.explanation: Cartwright's cognitive problem-solving view sees dreams as an extension of waking life that helps people work through emotional concerns. Activation-synthesis sees dream content as essentially random.

questions.stem: Crick and Mitchison's (1983) reverse learning theory proposes that during REM sleep the brain:
options: rehearses solutions to problems from the day
removes unwanted or unhelpful neural connections
fulfils unconscious wishes in a disguised form
repairs body tissue and releases growth hormone
questions.explanation: Crick and Mitchison proposed that REM sleep clears away unwanted, parasitic connections formed during the day, so 'we dream in order to forget'. Trying to remember dreams might therefore be unhelpful.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares Freud's theory of dreaming with activation-synthesis theory?
options: Both theories explain dreams as the removal of unwanted connections
Freud saw dreams as meaningful; activation-synthesis sees them as a by-product
Freud saw dreams as random; activation-synthesis sees them as hidden wishes
Both theories argue that dreams help solve the problems of waking life
questions.explanation: Freud's psychodynamic theory holds that dreams have deep meaning as disguised wishes. Activation-synthesis is a biological theory in which dreams are the cortex's attempt to interpret random brainstem activity.
